Albert Camus. An Algerian-French philosopher, novelist, and essayist whose work grapples with the absurdity of human existence—the collision between humanity's hunger for meaning and a universe indifferent to our search. Though often grouped with existentialists, Camus rejected that label, insisting that existentialism's emphasis on freedom and choice contradicted the fundamental meaninglessness he identified. He remains one of the twentieth century's most influential voices on alienation, rebellion, and how to live meaningfully in a senseless world. His novel The Stranger, published in nineteen forty-two, depicts Meursault, a man emotionally detached from life who commits a meaningless murder and faces execution with indifference. The novel's sparse prose and Meursault's emotional flatness embody absurdist alienation. The Myth of Sisyphus, also from nineteen forty-two, is Camus's philosophical essay on the absurd. He uses the myth of Sisyphus, a man condemned to eternally roll a boulder uphill, as a metaphor for human existence, arguing that we must imagine Sisyphus happy despite the futility. For Camus, the absurd is the collision between human rationality and the world's irrationality; it cannot be overcome by suicide, which he calls the central philosophical question, nor by false hope or the existentialist leap of faith. The Plague, published in nineteen forty-seven, is an allegorical novel about a plague-stricken North African city that explores solidarity, heroism, and the absurdity of suffering in a godless universe. Camus was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in nineteen fifty-seven at age forty-three, making him one of the youngest laureates; the prize recognized both his literary artistry and his moral philosophy. His philosophical and literary work refused clear political alignment: he broke with Jean-Paul Sartre over the Soviet Union and was skeptical of all ideologies that claimed to resolve the absurd. He was born in Algeria, which was the birthplace and setting for much of his fiction.
